processing: A cultivar rather than a processing style; as with most Japanese green tea it is normally steamed, rolled and dried as sencha.
harvest_season: First picking in spring, slightly ahead of Yabukita, by about two days in Saitama's own trait tables.
appearance_dry: As with other sencha, dark green, needle-like rolled leaf.
appearance_liquor: As typical of sencha, a clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Soft green broken leaf, typical of steamed sencha.
taste_profile: Little specific tasting detail is documented; expect the grassy, brisk, gently sweet character typical of Japanese sencha.

brewing.notes: Standard sencha parameters are the place to start; lengthen the first steep or add heat if the tea tastes thin.

vintage_note: As usual for Japanese green tea, it is sold as the current spring harvest and is best drunk within a year. It is mostly met inside Sayama-area teas, and a pack only names it when a farm sells it as a single cultivar.
description:
Sayamakaori is a green tea cultivar from Saitama, the home of Sayama tea, and it is one of the bushes the prefecture has recommended to its growers. Its registered name is Cha Norin 31.

It matters mainly to growers. It is hardy and high-yielding, enough to serve as the yardstick against which newer Saitama cultivars are measured, and it comes ready a little before Yabukita.

Detailed tasting notes are scarce. As with other sencha, brew around 75°C and expect a grassy, fresh cup; treat any specifics on a pack as that farm's own description.

If you find it named on a label, it is a nice way to taste a Saitama-bred bush rather than the ubiquitous Yabukita. Try it beside a Yabukita sencha from the same region if you can.
history: Sayamakaori was bred at the Saitama prefectural tea experiment station and adopted in 1971 among the prefecture's recommended cultivars. It later became a parent in the local breeding programme: Saitama's Ayanomidori descends from it, and the newer Sayama Akari is compared to it for yield.
